newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 22.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Treasurer Winston Peters said on Tuesday he was more concerned by the speed of the New Zealand dollar's rise than by the level it had reached. He refused to be drawn into the burgeoning debate over how to bring down the dollar's value, saying he was not yet ready. "It would be wrong to be stampeded into things. I have been in this job less than a week if you take the Christmas break out. I can be more effusive in a month from now." He said he would make a speech outlining his role as a treasurer on February 5 in Wellington. Page 1.

The Cook Islands government owes the New Zealand Government Superannuation Fund more than $6.5 million, according to the fund's briefing paper to the incoming government. The document highlights the risk to the government caused by the "situation with the Cook Islands and a substantial debt owing to the fund". It says the Cook Islands has not paid the employer subsidy for the superannuation scheme since July 1994. At October 31 last year, the fund was owed $6.532 million. Page 2.

The cabinet gathered on Tuesday for its first 1997 meeting with ministers aware they are behind schedule for the 1997-98 Budget as a result of the protracted coalition talks before Christmas. Prime Minister Jim Bolger said Tuesday's meeting -- which ran shorter than usual -- had had a "big" discussion of the economy. Much of ministers' initial Budget effort is going into meeting Treasurer Winston Peters's February 4 deadline to come up with possible savings in their departments. Page 2.

A mystery payment of almost $2 milllion allegedly involving some of New Zealand's top corporates is being investigated by the Serious Fraud Office. The Cook Islands tax commission of inquiry was told yesterday that Gib Beattie of the SFO had began an inquiry into what had become known as the "Laverton adjustment" when he was appointed assistant director of investigations four months ago. In evidence, Beattie said he had begun an investigation into the matter on behalf of the diretor Chas Sturt. Page 2.

Transport Minister Jenny Shipley has added her support to lowering the drinking age, but only if it is accompanied by harsher measures against drink drivers. Youth Affairs Minister Deborah Morris has called for a lowering of the drinking age from 20 to 18, partially because it is difficult for bar managers to judge young people's ages. Attorney-General Paul East has backed the call, but only if it is accompanied by photos on drivers' licences. Page 2.

The Agriculture Ministry yesterday issued a revised procedure for considering the rabbit calicivirus disease import application, aimed at getting more public comment and making the process more transparent. Ministry spokeswoman Debbie Gee said that in light of the large number of submissions received -- about 800 -- and the complexity of the issues raised, the ministry had decided to give submitters another opportunity to comment. Page 3.

The Agriculture Ministry was on Tuesday discussing export certification options with Australia after the discovery last Saturday of a microscopic mite in a shipment of apricots destined for Australia. The ministry's national export operations manager, Peter Johnston, said an agreement was not expected till tomorrow at the earliest, but he was confident of a positive outcome for exporters. Page 7.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger risks building a disaffected National backbench when he gives way to NZ First on everything from Cabinet posts to office space, former consumer affairs minister Katherine O'Regan said on Tuesday. O'Regan who was dropped as a minister in the post-coalition distribution of portfolios, said she had also been overlooked for a select committee chairmanship. Apart from diplomatic postings, select committee chairmanships are one of the few offerings Bolger has left to appease MPs either dumped from ministerial portfolios or who have failed to get the nod when the portfolios were handed out. Page 11.

Bank of New Zealand said it would issue an initial $90 million of commercial paper in its securitisation programme for Pacific Retail Group. Phillippe Blin, senior manager of BNZ's Structured Finance Group said about $30 million of paper would be offered to the market in each of three initial tenders on January 24, February 20 and March 20. "We'll be tapping the market over a period of time," he said. Under the scheme, the hire purchase portfolio of Pacific Retail -- the amalgamated Noel Leeming and Bond and Bond chains -- is assigned to a 100 percent subsidiary, Pacific Retail Finance. The debt is then
sold to a securitisation vehicle called Pacific Retail Securities. Page 18.

The Commerce Commission has cleared Alliance Textiles' purchase of two Feltex yarn plants -- to close them down. Alliance Textiles bought the plants in Fielding and Wainuiomata last year from BTR Nylex, and announced their closure with the loss of 100 jobs. BTR also sold the Feltex carpet business to senior managers and CS First Boston. The commission investigated Alliance's purchase of the two yarn plants because Alliance was already a force in the market. Page 18.

Massey University banking senior lecturer David Tripe's criticism of the Reserve Bank's disclosure regime was not founded, Reserve Bank banking system chief manager Peter Ledingham said on Tuesday. In an analysis of banks' results based on information published as a result of disclosure requirements, Tripe said a weakness of the disclosure regime was "that there is no requirement for banks to identify their exposures" to fixed and capped-rate loans. Page 18.

Two New Zealand firms with investments in Chile have no plans to list on the Chilean Stock Exchange when the law is changed soon to allow foreign firms to list. Bloomberg reported on Tuesday that Chile Finance Minister Eduardo Aninant signed a bill allowing shares of foreign companies to be traded on the exchange. The bill will be sent to the congress for approval after gaining the presidential nod. Page 18.

Tomorrow's September 1996 gross domestic product numbers are so historical that the markets are unlikely to react, but economists say they will look for upward revisions in previous data to explain stronger inflation. Last Friday, Statistics New Zealand figures showed inflation above market figures and Reserve Bank expectations, at 2.6 percent headline and 2.4 percent underlying. "The numbers to focus on are what they do to the revisions to the year to March 1996," Bankers Trust economist David Plank said. Page 19.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

The head of the Auckland police Asian crime unit has backed a call for a special task force to battle triad gangs, saying they are already well established in New Zealand and are terrorising parts of the Asian community. And a Hong Kong police officer has warned New Zealand authorities they must move to stamp out the menace now before it permeates into "mainstream" New Zealand. On Tuesday Labour justice spokesman Phil Goff called for a multi-agency task force to stamp out Asian triad gangs.

Exporters' hopes for a drop in the dollar now hinge on the Governor of the Reserve Bank, Dr Don Brash, after the government's refusal on Tuesday to get involved. The Prime Minister confirmed that the issue had been discussed in Tuesday's cabinet meeting -- the first of the New Year -- and acknowledged the "harm" it was causing the export sector but indicated that the government's hands were tied.

High fuel costs and the strong dollar have analysts set to lower their forecasts for Air New Zealand's June 1997 profit. Latest indications suggest that the carrier's earnings will be around $180 million -- assuming that jet fuel prices fall and the dollar softens. Expectations for this year started at around $200 million after a 13 percent slump in June 1996 year earnings to $225 million was announced last September. In December, that figure was lowered to a market average of $190 million.

There were no plans to cash in on the strength of the All Blacks brand through a stock exchange listing, the New Zealand Rugby Union said on Tuesday. "It is not on the agenda," said the chief executive, David Moffett. The possibility had been discussed very briefly by the rugby union board as part of its strategic planning process. "But we are not about to go and list."

The Loaded Hog chain of bars and boutique breweries may soon expand oversease after a recent change of ownership. Simon Meikle, who bought the Loaded Hog Group in a joint ventrue with the Emerald Group, said Australia was the logical place for overseas expansion of the chain. The Emerald Group is a private investment company associated with the Foreman family, who sold Trigon Industries to United States based Sealed Air in 1994. It also has a stake of about five percent in Ernest Adams.

The 90-day bank bill yield, a key influence on banks' mortgage rates, fell nine points to a 28-month low on Tuesday as financial markets noted then ignored comments from politicians. As the 90-day yield dropped, the New Zealand dollar rebounded fom an early fall to finish, on a trade-weighted index basis, unchanged from Monday at 68.6.

The Commerce Commission has cleared Alliance Textiles to buy Feltex's yarn operations. The commission said that, while Alliance would be the biggest producer of industrial and hand knitting yarns following the buy, competition from six other

producers would prevent it from acquiring or strengthening market dominancy. If Alliance tried to use its market power the other New Zealand producers could respond by changing their production to meet customers' needs.

September 1996 gross domestic product figures, to be released tomorrow, are too old for markets to be likely to react, say economists. They also say they will be looking fo upward revisions in previous data to explain stronger inflation. On Friday, Statistics New Zealand figures showed inflation above market and Reserve Bank expectations, at 2.6 percent headline
and 2.4 percent underlying.

Statistics New Zealand is working to improve the timelines of quarterly gross domestic product statistics, which it concedes are too old when released. "We would like to see an improvement in the timelines this year. That would be our goal," its senior economic statistician, Stephen Hickson, said. "At the moment we're investigating the possibility of bringing forward the release from 13 weeks after the reference quarter, which is what it currently is, to somewhere around ten or 11, which is comparable to many other countries."

Massey University banking lecturer David Tripe's criticism of the Reserve Bank's disclosure regime was ill-founded, Reserve Bank banking system chief manager Peter Ledingham says. In an analysis of banks' results based on information published under the disclosure requirements, Tripe said a weakness of the regime was the lack of a requirement for banks to identify exposures to fixed and capped rate loans.
